desc:
The tree below was meant to be a binary search tree but may contain mistakes. Call a node misplaced if it breaks the order demanded by at least one of its ancestors: it lies in the left subtree of an ancestor but its value is not smaller than that ancestor, or it lies in the right subtree of an ancestor but its value is not larger than that ancestor. Equal values therefore count as a violation.

Return the number of misplaced nodes. A tree is a valid BST exactly when the answer is 0. Every ancestor counts, even an ancestor that is itself misplaced.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14] is the tree whose root 8 has children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6; node 10 has no left child and right child 14.

Example 1

tree = [10,5,15,-1,-1,6,20]
Output: 1
The node 6 is the left child of 15, but it also lies in the right subtree of 10 and 6 < 10.

Example 2

tree = [3,4,2,5]
Output: 3
The node 4 is in the left subtree of 3 but is larger; 2 is in the right subtree of 3 but is smaller; and 5 sits in the left subtree of 3 as well, below 4, and is larger than 3.

Example 3

tree = [2,1,3]
Output: 0
hints: Comparing a node with its parent is not enough, as Example 1 shows. A node must respect every ancestor.
While going down, every ancestor that you pass on the left side gives an upper bound, every ancestor passed on the right gives a lower bound. Only the tightest bounds matter.

Do a stack walk carrying (node, lo, hi). A node is misplaced if it is not strictly between lo and hi. Children inherit (lo, min(hi, value)) and (max(lo, value), hi) from their parent, whether or not the parent was misplaced.
editorial: Each ancestor restricts its descendants: everything on its left must be smaller and everything on its right larger. Accumulating these restrictions along the path gives for each node an open interval (lo, hi), where lo is the largest ancestor value from which we went right and hi the smallest ancestor value from which we went left. A node violates some ancestor exactly when its value is not strictly inside that interval.

Note that the bounds must keep being tightened by the node's own value even if the node is misplaced, because the definition counts every ancestor. One depth-first walk with an explicit stack does the job in O(n) time, O(n) space, and does not recurse so deep trees are fine.
